issues.legal_issue: The evidence was insufficient to establish the accused persons’ responsibility for the abduction or death of the deceased through common intention.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on a witness’s account that he saw three people carrying a body and throwing it into a canal, and identifying the body as the deceased from a distance of about eight kanals at about 6 a.m.
The witness’s account of what he did after seeing the event contained contradictions and improvements, and the High Court had declined to rely on it against one of the alleged participants.
The prosecution had no other evidence showing when or where the deceased was murdered or how the body was disposed of.
After rejecting the disposal witness’s account, the Court considered it unsafe to rely on the other witnesses’ evidence that the accused persons abducted or murdered the deceased.
issues.conclusion: The accused persons could not be held responsible for the deceased’s abduction or death by applying common intention, and the convictions on that basis could not be sustained.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove criminal responsibility beyond reasonable doubt. The Court considered the charges concerning abduction and murder, including Sections 364 and 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, and held that the unreliable evidence about disposal of the body made it unsafe to rely on the related evidence of abduction or murder. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The accused appealed against their criminal convictions.
predicates.disposal_witness_unreliable: A witness whose account was relied on to establish disposal of the body gave an account containing serious reliability problems, including contradictions or improvements.
predicates.fatal_involvement_depended_on_disposal_a: The evidence connecting the accused to the abduction or death was not independently reliable once the disposal account was rejected.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns criminal convictions and the unreliable disposal account is essential to the evidence of fatal involvement, the accused are not held responsible for the abduction or death.

issues.legal_issue: Direct testimony from an injured witness established that the accused persons intentionally caused injuries to that witness with weapons, making them guilty of voluntary hurt with common intention.
material_facts: The injured witness testified that one accused struck him above the left ear with a gandasa and that the other struck his finger with a dang.
The Court accepted the injured witness’s account of the assaults and rejected the contention that the injuries could have been self-inflicted.
The Court treated the evidence of the assaults as proved beyond reasonable doubt even though the remaining prosecution case concerning the incident could not be relied on.
issues.conclusion: The accused persons were convicted under Section 324 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to three years’ rigorous imprisonment; if they had served that sentence, they were entitled to remission and release, provided they were not wanted in another case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the accepted testimony of the injured witness to find that the accused voluntarily caused hurt using a gandasa and a dang. It applied Sections 324 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The accused appealed against their criminal convictions.
predicates.injured_witness_identified_each_assailan: An injured witness directly identified each accused as having caused an injury to the witness.
predicates.self_infliction_claim_lacked_support: The claim that the injuries were self-inflicted was not supported by the circumstances accepted by the court.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns criminal convictions, an injured witness directly identifies each assailant, and the claim of self-infliction lacks support, the accused are convicted of voluntary hurt with common intention.
